Species turnover and nestedness are two distinct components used to break down and understand beta diversity—which measures how much species composition changes between different communities or sites [@baselga2010], where, turnover is the replacement of some species by different species from one site to another, while nestedness is the loss or gain of species where poorer sites contain a strict subset of the species found at richer sites. CITAR: [@ligeiro2010; @crist2003; @ávila2011; @shell2018; @baselga2012; @baselga2010; @gering2003; @veech2003] ## Objectives This study describes the richness and density of zooplankton, comparatively between two small head water streams subject to different levels of environmental pressures. One originates withing a protected area - Biological Reserve, or REBIO, according to @brasil2000 - and its course extends beyond its administrative boundaries [@mma2003], and a second one that flows entirely outside of the protected area. Within this framework, we use hierarchical additive partitioning to evaluate the relative contribution of different spatial and temporal scales to the diversity of zooplankton assemblages. Given the importance of the Atlantic Forest to the biodiversity [@pereira2026] and its fragmented stated north of the São Francisco river basin [@silva2003], we aim with this study, (1) to infer environmental degradation from species turnover [@baselga2010] and (2) to associate beta-diversity to the ecological health of sites inside and surrounding a protected area of Atlantic Forest. Given the expected different levels of environmental pressures in the area [@gouveia2017], we hypothesize that the diversity is not be homogeneously distributed among the different spatial scales but concentrated at the finer levels and seasonal variation will be limited to species composition, but no spacial variation is expected between dry and wet seasons. Some environmental features (reach morphology, habitat structure, and water quality) are also described to explore possible explaining factors for the observed patterns. # Material and methods ## Study area and sampling design This study was conducted in the Guaribas Biological Reserve (REBIO Guaribas), a protected area of Atlantic Forest in northeastern Brazil. This protected area is located in a transitional zone between the Caatinga and Atlantic Forest ecoregions. The land use of the study area is based on the occupation of traditional human populations and an increasing use of land for large scale monocultures, mostly sugar cane [@heinrichs2017]. Other than these, small scale agricultural activities, fishing, and the modification of the natural vegetation for livestock are important anthropogenic pressures that affect the buffer zone of the REBIO [@arruda2013; @mma2026]. Other common uses of the soil in the area are, coconut plantations, orchards and subsistence agriculture. These land uses represent important sources of pollution, either through agrochemicals runoff or direct and indirect domestic effluents (such as septic tanks). These nonpoint source pollutants contaminate underground water and create a spatial gradient of environmental disturbance [@mehla2026]. Therefore, the mainly rural nature of the land use associated with the management of vegetation, will cause direct impact to aquatic systems, by the siltation of streams and contamination of groundwater. The hydrographic network of the study region is composed predominantly of small catchments containing first- and second-order streams [@strahler1957 classification] (@fig-mapa). These watercourses are tributaries of the Camaratuba River and are sustained by numerous springs distributed throughout the region. The two main stream systems in the study area are the Barro Branco and Caiana catchemnts. The Barro Branco stream is approximately 8.8 km long and originates within the protected area. Its upper section remains within the boundaries of the REBIO, whereas its middle and lower sections extend into the surrounding landscape. Despite this transition, riparian vegetation is preserved along most of the stream. The Caiana stream is approximately 9.8 km long and also originates within the REBIO, although most of its course lies outside the protection area. The climate in the region is classified as As' [@peel2007], characterized by a mean annual temperature of approximately 25 °C, with maximum temperatures occurring mainly between February and March, during the dry period, as well as by low annual thermal amplitude. Annual precipitation ranges from 1,400 to 1,800 mm, concentrated between March and July, whereas the lowest rainfall levels occur between September and December. In the study area, rainfall is concentrated between March and July, beginning in autumn and extending into winter. This pattern is attributed to the influence of cold air masses from the South Atlantic ocean that affect the region. The hydrographic network is composed of small headwater streams fed by rain [@gouveia2017]. A total of 15 sampling sites distributed longitudinally across the two Atlantic Forest streams were selected to capture spatial variation in environmental conditions and habitat characteristics. The Barro Branco stream included sampling sites located within a protected area (REBIO Guaribas) and sites located outside its boundaries, whereas all sampling sites in the Caiana stream were located outside the protected area. This sampling design allowed the assessment of zooplankton diversity across nested spatial scales and contrasting conditions of environmental protection and human influence (@fig-mapa). Sampling included temporal (dry and wet seasons) and spatial scales. The spatial scales of zooplankton diversity were represented by the total gamma (γ) diversity, encompassing both study streams. At each stream, several sites were selected according to their position in the main channel of the catchment basin and, at each site, three habitas were sampled to represent different habitat types (pool, riffle, near underwater structures) [@frissell1986]. We also considered a further spatial scale being the upper reaches (portion of the Barro Branco stream within the conservation unit and the Caiana stream before its confluence with the Pipina stream) and the lower reaches (portion of the Barro Branco stream outside the conservation unit and the Caiana stream after its confluence with the Pipina stream) (@fig-mapa). Sampling was conducted during the dry (January-February) and wet (June-July) seasons of 2024. ## Environmental data collection Environmental conditions were characterized using four groups of variables, following procedures adapted by @medeiros2008 from the protocols proposed by @pusey2004 and @mugodo2006: site morphology, water quality, substrate composition, and marginal habitat structure. Morphological characteristics were assessed from three randomly selected transects at each site, where stream width (cm) and water depth (cm) were measured. Bank slope was classified into four categories according to its inclination: 1, ≤ 20°; 2, \> 20–30°; 3, \> 30–50°; and 4, \> 50°. Broader-scale landscape characteristics, including elevation and stream length, were obtained from handheld GPS records and satellite imagery. Water quality was characterized using physical and chemical measurements obtained with portable instruments, including water temperature (°C) and dissolved oxygen concentration (mg/L). Turbidity was subsequently measured in the laboratory with a turbidimeter using water samples collected at each sampling site. Current velocity (m/s) was estimated using the float method, as described by @maitland1990. Substrate composition and the physical structure of marginal habitats were evaluated from 9 to 12 quadrats (1 m²) distributed along the terrestrial-aquatic interface at each sampling site. Within each quadrat, the proportional cover of different substrate categories was visually estimated, including mud, sand, cobbles, small and large gravel and rocks. The same quadrats were used to characterize littoral and submerged habitat features. Recorded habitat components included macrophytes, marginal grasses, leaf litter, attached and filamentous algae, overhanging and submerged vegetation, small and large woody debris, and root masses [@medeiros2008]. For subsequent analyses and presentation, environmental measurements were summarized as mean values for each sampling site. Three 250 mL replicate samples of water from each site were taken and refrigerated for concentration analysis (μg L⁻¹) of ammonia, nitrite, nitrate, orthophosphate (soluble reactive phosphorus) and total phosphorus. Nutrient concentrations were obtained based on Standard Methods for the Examination of Water [-@apha1998] and @mackereth1978. ## Zooplankton sampling Zooplankton was sampled at habitats within each sampling site, hereafter referred to as habitat samples. Collections were performed in the main channel of the streams at the surface water. At each sampling habitat, a plankton net (30 cm mouth diameter, 70 cm length, and 60 μm mesh size) was used to filter 50 L of water. The net was rinsed between successive samples to prevent clogging and carryover of organisms. Each sample was concentrated to a final volume of 80 mL for laboratory analyses. Following collection, zooplankton samples were anesthetized with commercial sparkling water and subsequently preserved in 4% formalin [@epa2020]. Sucrose was added to the preserved sample to prevent female cladocerans from losing eggs and to minimize carapace distortion [@haney1973]. In the laboratory, samples had their zooplankton identified and counted using a Sedgewick–Rafter counting chamber. The analyses focused on representatives of Rotifera, Cladocera, and Copepoda. Taxonomic identification was based on specialized literature and confirmed by specialists. To evaluate whether the sampling effort adequately represented the zooplankton assemblage, species accumulation curves were calculated [@lucena2015; @melo2014]. ## Statistical analyses Environmental variables were screened for multicollinearity and to identify redundant descriptors. Variables representing similar environmental information were also combined when appropriate, thereby reducing redundancy in the dataset [@legendre1998]. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code summarize multivariate patterns of environmental variation among sampling sites. Prior to PCA, site morphology and water-quality variables were square-root transformed [@sokal1995]. Variables describing sediment composition and marginal habitat structure, expressed as percentages, were relativized by their column totals and subsequently subjected to the arcsine square-root transformation [@mccune2002]. PCA was conducted in R using the `FactoMineR` package [@lê2008], with all variables centered and standardized to unit variance before analysis. The water quality parameters temperature and dissolved oxygen, and all nutrients were used to characterize differences between streams but were not used in the PCA because they were not measured for both seasons. A Permutational Multivariate Analysis of Variance (PERMANOVA, 999 permutations) was performed to test whether the overall set of environmental variables measured differed across the seasons and streams [@freiry2020; @anderson2013]. Zooplankton diversity was characterized using species richness (R) and Shannon's density (D) [@magurran2013]. Species richness was calculated as the number of species recorded in each sample, whereas density was expressed as the number of individuals per liter (ind./L) [@bowen2017; @silva2017]. Variation in richness and density was evaluated using factorial analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by *post hoc* multiple comparisons using Tukey’s HSD test (α=0.05) [@zar2010]. Density was square root transformed to enhance normality and homogeneity of variances [@sokal1995] and species richness was corrected based on rarefied analyses for the average number of individuals from all sites [@chao2014; @oksanen; @medeiros2024]. Each observation was classified according to three factors: river reach (three levels), habitat (three levels), and hydrological season (wet and dry). The analysis initially considered the full factorial model. When significant interactions were detected, higher-order interactions were examined first, followed by the corresponding two-way interactions (reach × season, reach × habitat, and season × habitat) and, subsequently, the main effects. Response variables were transformed using log₁₀(x + 1) to improve compliance with assumptions of normality and homogeneity of variances \[39\]. Differences among factor levels were subsequently investigated using Tukey's HSD test at α = 0.05. Differences in assemblage composition across the spatial hierarchy and seasons were explored using the Unweighted Pair Group Method with Averages (UPGMA) [@belbin1993; @diniz-reis2022], based on Bray-Curtis dissimilarities calculated from the zooplankton density matrix [@ávila2011]. Prior to the analyses, density data were relativized and square-root transformed to reduce the influence of highly abundant taxa and improve the distributional properties of the dataset [@rocha2012]. To focus on spatial variation across sampling sites, habitat density data were pooled for this analysis. To assess how well the UPGMA dendrograms represented the original Bray-Curtis dissimilarities among sampling sites, the Cophenetic Correlation Coefficient (CC) was calculated [@sneath1973; @sokal1962; @saraçli2013], where a cophenetic matrix was constructed from each seasonal dendrogram using the *cophenetic* function in the `vegan` package in R. The cophenetic distance matrix was then correlated with the corresponding original Bray-Curtis dissimilarity matrix using Pearson's product-moment correlation coefficient [@farris1969; @silva2013; @sokal1962]. To evaluate the strength of the hierarchical clustering structure obtained from the UPGMA dendrograms, the Agglomerative Coefficient (AC) was calculated for each season using the *coef.hclust* function from the `cluster` package in R [@maechler2026; @kaufman1990]. The AC ranges from 0 to 1, where values closer to 1 indicate a strong, well-defined clustering structure and values near 0 reflect weak or indistinct grouping. Additive diversity partitioning was used to quantify the contribution of within- and between-unit diversity to total zooplankton diversity. In this framework, alpha diversity ($\alpha$) represents diversity occurring within sampling units, whereas beta diversity ($\beta$) represents the contribution of differences among units at successive levels of the spatial hierarchy [@lande1996; @crist2003]. The hierarchical structure included three spatial scales. The finest scales consisted of the habitat samples within each site (n = 3), and of each site (n = 6, for the Barro Branco stream, and n = 9, for the Caiana stream). The intermediate scales corresponded to the upper and lower stream sections (n = 2), whereas the broadest scale represented differences among the two streams. Accordingly, the total diversity (γ) was decomposed into within-habitat diversity (α₁) and the successive beta components associated with differences among habitats (𝛽₁), among sites withing upper and lower stream reaches (β₂), and among streams (β₃). The contribution of each component was expressed as a percentage of total diversity [@crist2003; @farias2020]. To investigate seasonal variation in the hierarchical structure of diversity, additive partitioning was performed separately for each season and for each stream [@farias2020; @melo2013]. The overall diversity was taken to be the sum of the relative contributions of each scale in the hierarchical sampling design. Analysis of significance of the contribution of each hierarchical level was performed through with individual-based randomizations (type I null model) [see @freiry2020; @melo2013]. The randomization process was repeated 999 times to obtain null distributions of the α and β diversity at each hierarchical level, and used to test whether the observed values were higher or lower than expected by chance [@crist2003] . The probabilities obtained from randomization tests were interpreted as *P*-values, as a low *P*-value (Prop~exp~ \> Prop~obs~ \< 0.05) indicates an observed diversity significantly different than that expected under the null model.
